(1) ASSESSMENT RATE = max(product rate + APRA buffer, lender floor), which is what the page's own FAQ promises ('APRA requires lenders to add a serviceability buffer of at least 3.00 percentage points to the product rate, and most lenders also apply a floor... your repayment capacity is tested at whichever is higher'). On the shipped dials that is max(5.90+3.00, 5.50) = 8.90%. (2) PERIOD RATE is nominal, annual/12, the universal Australian mortgage convention and the one TESTCASES Z1/F1 records as the repo norm outside financingvscash. At 8.90% the monthly rate is 0.089/12 = 0.0074166667 and the 360-month annuity factor (1-(1+i)^-n)/i is 125.401630. Under the effective convention (1.089^(1/12)-1) the factor would be 129.7276, about 3.4% higher, so every capacity in this file would be understated by that much - that is the diagnosis if the capacities fail high by ~3.4% in lockstep. (3) CAPACITY = the loan a level in-arrears P&I repayment supports over the full term at the assessment rate, found by BISECTION on ref.annuity_payment (ref.annuity_principal_bisect), never by the closed-form present-value formula, so the expectation is not the same algebra a calculator would naturally run. That last formula is corroborated by the page's own first-home-buyer Quick Start tooltip: $70,000 saved less the $4,000 of other purchase costs is $66,000, and $66,000 x 0.8/0.2 = $264,000, the capacity that tooltip quotes. (12) MAX PURCHASE PRICE = capacity + available funds, per the Max purchase price tooltip ('capacity plus the deposit left over'). (13) LMI: the premium is lmiRate x the advance and is capitalised, so the debt serviced is advance x (1 + lmiRate) and the capacity reported is the advance. (14) HEM is not published anywhere on the page, so no expectation in this file states a HEM dollar figure. Fixtures either set declared expenses above any plausible HEM (so living costs are exactly the declared figure) or test HEM only through ratios and orderings. (15) Money tolerances of +/-550 on a capacity and +/-1,100 on a difference of two capacities exist to allow rounding to the nearest whole $1,000; they are far tighter than any convention error this file is designed to catch.

The study-loan tooltip: 'both paths subtract the same dollars from surplus income. The difference is where it lands.' As tax it comes off net income; as a commitment it is added to outgoings; the UMI test subtracts the same $662.50/mo either way, so the capacity must be identical to the dollar.

With N net income, O other outgoings, H the study loan and R the repayment, the tax path gives NSR = (N-H)/(O+R) and the commitment path N/(O+H+R). Cross-multiplying, the difference has the sign of H x (N - O - H - R), and N - O - H - R is the surplus left over, which is the $250 minimum UMI. So the tax path must show the HIGHER NSR whenever the minimum UMI is positive - the same money, a different ratio, which is exactly the distinction the tooltip draws.
On the tax path the study loan sits above the line, so the commitments table must not also carry it.
On the commitment path it sits below the line as $7,950/12 = $662.50/mo of commitments.
